Ray: Good morning, nerds! It's Thursday, November twelfth, twenty twenty-six, and this is Nerd News Radio.

Lead story

Ray: Okay, so the Ising model is the classic toy magnet. Little spins that point up or down, and neighbors want to line up. Physicists love it because it shows a critical point, where the system flips from disordered to ordered.

Ada: And hyperbolic lattices? Those are tilings of a negatively curved surface, right?

Ray: Right. Regular tilings where the number of sites near the edge grows as fast as the interior. The paper calls them non-amenable lattices. In plain words, the boundary never becomes negligible, so how you treat the edge really matters.

Ray: The authors ran Monte Carlo simulations, using worm and Metropolis methods, on four hyperbolic tilings. They compared open boundaries with wired boundaries, where every edge spin couples to one shared auxiliary spin.

Ada: So what did they actually find?

Ray: With open boundaries, the susceptibility, basically how strongly the system responds to a nudge, follows finite-size scaling based on volume. The exponents are not mean-field, and they're roughly stable across all four tilings. That hints at a common universality class. But Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks show substantial finite-size effects.

Ada: Okay, skeptic hat. Is this a simulation or an experiment?

Ray: Simulation. Nothing was measured in a real material.

Ada: And a common universality class, is that proven?

Ray: No. The abstract says the results support the possibility. That's careful wording.

Ada: What about the wired case?

Ray: There, the correlator between the central spin and the auxiliary spin shows radial scaling consistent with a mean-field magnetization exponent. The central spin's response to a uniform field is consistent with delta equals three. And a weak boundary field produces magnetization that is enhanced toward the interior.

Ada: So same lattice, different edges, different critical picture.

Ray: Exactly. The takeaway is that interior and whole-system measurements can disagree. If you use scaling analysis to find critical points, that matters. The abstract doesn't say whether this carries to real materials, so we'll leave that open.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets. First, a chain-like van der Waals antiferromagnet, silver chromium phosphorus two sulfur six.

Ada: Mouthful. What did they get?

Ray: From susceptibility, a classical Fisher chain fit gives an intrachain exchange, the coupling between neighboring spins, of about one hundred forty kelvin. A quantum spin three halves chain fit gives about one hundred fourteen kelvin. Nuclear magnetic resonance on phosphorus adds that below the ordering temperature, relaxation follows temperature to the fifth power, consistent with magnons. The critical exponent beta is about zero point three six, consistent with three-dimensional behavior.

Ada: So the coupling depends on which model you pick.

Ray: Yes, and the authors settle on a scale of order one hundred kelvin.

Ray: Next, tetrataenite, an ordered iron nickel phase studied as a rare-earth-free magnet candidate. A journal listing came out this month, but no abstract was available, so we can't tell you the findings.

Ada: Then I'll just say the question to watch is whether it stays ordered at useful temperatures.

Ray: Fair. And one for the simulation crowd. A new discrete model reproduces the multichannel Kondo model exactly, and cluster Monte Carlo algorithms completely eliminate critical slowing down.

Ada: Which is when simulations crawl near a critical point.

Ray: Yes. Smarter update rules, much cheaper physics.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Here's my favorite. A frustration-free Hamiltonian is one whose ground state minimizes every local energy term at once. A new paper proves you can decide whether one is frustration-free at all sizes, because there's a finite size cutoff.

Ising model on hyperbolic lattices: boundary conditions change the critical story

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports Monte Carlo simulations of the ferromagnetic Ising model on four hyperbolic tilings, using worm and Metropolis methods. With open boundaries, susceptibility follows volume-based finite-size scaling with non-mean-field exponents, and Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks show large finite-size effects. The likely takeaway is that interior and whole-system measurements can give different pictures, which matters for anyone using scaling analysis to locate critical points.

America Makes, the US federal additive manufacturing institute, has released a roadmap focused on 3D printing for space propulsion. Only the headline from The Manila Times was available, so the roadmap's contents are unconfirmed. Roadmaps like this often shape future funding calls and research priorities.

Colorado rare-earth bid targets China's estimated 94% permanent-magnet share

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 7/10

A Colorado effort is aiming at China's estimated 94% share of permanent-magnet production. No body text was available, so the specifics are unconfirmed. The story reflects the broader push to reduce dependence on a single supplier for the magnets used in motors, generators and electronics.

AgCrP2S6 susceptibility and NMR give an intrachain exchange scale near 100 K

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports an intrachain exchange coupling J/kB of about 140 K from a classical Fisher-chain fit and 114 K from a quantum S=3/2 chain fit. It also reports a critical exponent β≈0.36, consistent with 3D universality. The example shows how magnetic interaction strengths can be pulled out of experimental data, and the value depends on which model is chosen for the fit.

Track-height control for DED on porous substrates starts with system identification

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 7/10

The abstract describes a conceptual approach to controlling track height in directed energy deposition on porous substrates: first identify the process dynamics, then evaluate control strategies that fit the process. It is about DED rather than laser powder bed fusion, and no results are quoted. It is a useful example of how closed-loop control of metal printing begins with modeling how the process behaves over time.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Spin supersolid in an easy-axis triangular XXZ antiferromagnet, via parton theory

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a fermionic parton mean-field and RPA study of the easy-axis spin-1/2 XXZ model on a triangular lattice. It finds Y and Y' states and a roton minimum at the M point. The easy axis is built into the model rather than measured in a specific material, but the work shows how anisotropy shapes the excitations.

Thermal stability of tetrataenite (L1_0 FeNi) for rare-earth-free magnets

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 6/10

Tetrataenite, an ordered iron-nickel phase, is being studied as a candidate permanent magnet that avoids rare earth elements. No abstract was available, so its findings are unconfirmed. The question of whether it stays ordered at useful temperatures is central to whether it could ever replace rare-earth magnets.

Cluster Monte Carlo for the Kondo model removes critical slowing down

Physical Review Letters · 6/10

The abstract reports a discrete model that reproduces the multichannel Kondo model and is simulated with cluster algorithms that eliminate critical slowing down. The Kondo model describes magnetic impurities in a metal rather than a crystal lattice. It is a good reminder of how smarter update rules can make simulations near critical points far more efficient.

Deconfined quantum criticality found in a dissipative spin-1/2 chain

Physical Review Letters · 6/10

The abstract reports non-Abelian bosonization, renormalization group and quantum Monte Carlo results. It finds continuous transitions between antiferromagnetic and valence-bond-solid order, with spinon deconfinement and an emergent O(4) symmetry in the Ohmic case. It is a one-dimensional theoretical model with no direct materials link.

Theoretical Physics

Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

A frustration-free Hamiltonian is one whose ground state minimizes every local term at once, as in the AKLT and toric-code models. The abstract reports a finite size cutoff beyond which frustration-freeness at that size guarantees it at all sizes, which makes the question decidable. But the cutoff is uncomputable as a function of local dimension, and one frustration-free Hamiltonian cannot be proven so in ZFC, so an answer can exist without anyone being able to prove it.

Toric-code leakage to a strip maps onto the random-bond Ising Nishimori point

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract proves that an observer's advantage in learning a logical bit equals 1 − 2P_fail. The strip's operational threshold is located at the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, found with a transfer matrix to within a few thousandths. It is a case where a classic statistical-physics point shows up inside an error-correction problem.

Analytic bounds on conformal defects constrain impurity order in O(N) models

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract derives bounds on defect scaling dimensions from the conformal bootstrap. For pinning-field defects, the bounds rule out stable impurity order with three or more orientations in O(2) and O(3) models. In other words, they limit what kinds of order can survive when a pinned impurity sits at a critical point.

Proposal to test whether gravity entangles a levitated particle with nuclear clocks

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

The abstract proposes an experiment in which a micrometer-scale levitated particle interacts with an array of nuclear clocks. A positive result would require clock energy to contribute to active gravitational mass, which would be evidence that active gravitational mass is quantized, a property that has not been tested. It is a proposal rather than a measurement, and it asks whether gravity behaves quantum mechanically.
